content: I'll start by reading the test image to identify the key visual features.

The test image shows: stem/crown area with **white cottony/fluffy mycelial growth** on two areas of decayed stems, brown rotted stem tissue, and visible roots. This pattern is characteristic of fungal stem rot diseases. Top candidates: Southern Blight, Sclerotinia Timber Rot, Gray Mold.

Now I can synthesize my analysis across all 8 views.

**Test image key features:**
- Prominent **bright white fluffy/cottony mycelial growth** at two distinct stem points
- Brown/tan decayed stem tissue beneath the white growth
- Uprooted plant with roots and soil visible against black background
- Green stem tissue still present in some areas

**Reference image comparison:**
- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot (Bugwood_14)**: Best visual match — showed white fluffy mycelium on stem segments with dark sclerotia, very similar to the test image's white cottony growth
- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot (Bugwood_19)**: Showed brown stem cankers at base with roots — similar overall setting but lacking visible white mycelium
- **Southern_Blight (3 images)**: All showed wilting/crown rot without the prominent white mycelial masses seen in test image
- **Gray_Mold (Bugwood_1)**: Microscopic view, not comparable
- **Phytophthora_Blight (Bugwood_10)**: Dark lesions, no white mycelium — doesn't match

The white cottony mycelium growing externally on multiple stem points is the defining feature here. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum produces exactly this dense, white, fluffy external mycelium on infected stems, and the Bugwood_14 reference was the strongest visual match to the test image.
